draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did he add the cash to conceal the one-million-yen amount by making it impossible to tell how much money was in the bag?"}
review: The proposal overstates the evidence: “impossible to tell” is stronger than the prior “yes” that adding cash changed what attackers could infer. The “no” only says exceeding one million wasn’t important; it doesn’t establish that the goal was to obscure the exact amount. A more discriminating question: “Was the added cash meant to make the bag seem less conspicuous to potential attackers, rather than to make its exact contents harder to estimate?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the added cash intended to make the amount in the bag less predictable to a potential attacker?"}

We know the extra cash changed what attackers could infer, but making the total exceed ¥1 million was not important, and making the amount less predictable was rejected. A more discriminating question: “Was the change in attackers’ inference caused by the bag’s outward appearance, such as its size or weight, rather than by a feature of the money itself?”

The outside-circumstances and outward-cue questions were irrelevant, so neither identifies the mechanism. review: The proposed question bundles two unsupported specifics: that the extra cash was withdrawn Japanese currency and that it remained exchangeable for yen. The history establishes only that its legal treatment affected ordinary payment; it does not identify the mechanism. It also already rules out foreign currency, counterfeit/invalid money, and valid Japanese currency with unusual ordinary-payment acceptance. A cleaner discriminator is: “Could the added cash be redeemed or exchanged for ordinary yen, even though it could not be spent directly?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Could the added cash be redeemed or exchanged for ordinary yen, even though it could not be spent directly?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the extra cash made up of Japanese banknotes that had been withdrawn from circulation and were no longer legal tender?"}
review: The proposal jumps to a specific explanation—withdrawn Japanese banknotes—without support from the feedback. That does not establish that the notes had been withdrawn from circulation or ceased to be legal tender. Several specific avenues have already been ruled out, including foreign currency, counterfeit/invalid money, and currency with a transaction-use restriction, so don’t treat stamps as the solution. A broader discriminating question would be: “Did the added items have an officially assigned monetary value but were not currency usable for ordinary purchases?”

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the added cash made up of banknotes or coins that had been withdrawn from circulation and were no longer legal tender?"}

That makes “withdrawn from circulation and no longer legal tender” particularly unlikely. A better next question would clarify the remaining broad distinction without presupposing a mechanism: “Did the legal treatment of the added cash matter for a reason other than whether it could be spent as ordinary payment?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the legal treatment of the added cash matter for a reason other than whether it could be spent as ordinary payment?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the added cash made up of banknotes or coins that had been withdrawn from circulation or demonetized, so they were no longer legal tender?"}
review:
I would not ask the proposed question: whether the extra cash was invalid or otherwise not spendable currency was already answered “no,” and demonetized notes would fall under that rejected idea. Several related avenues—foreign currency, restrictions on payment, lack of redemption, and other legal treatment—were also rejected. The history therefore does not support naming a specific kind of cash, and its mixed answers do not establish a mechanism.

A more discriminating question would be: “Did the added cash’s legal status affect the consequences for a would-be robber if caught with it, rather than whether the cash could be spent or exchanged?” If the answer is no, avoid a final explanation that invents another legal distinction; the current history is not enough to reconstruct the reason.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the added cash’s legal status affect the consequences for a would-be robber if caught with it, rather than whether the cash could be spent or exchanged?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the added cash legally valid Japanese banknotes or coins, but in a condition that made them difficult or impossible to use for ordinary purchases?"}
review:
The proposed question is probably redundant: the history already got “no” to whether valid Japanese currency was different in a way that affected everyday acceptance, and “no” to several other spendability/use explanations. The “yes” answers establish that a feature of the added cash and its legal status mattered, but they do not establish that physical condition was that feature. Mixed feedback also makes it unsafe to infer a specific mechanism.

A better discriminating question: “Was the relevant legal distinction about the cash’s classification or attached rights, rather than its physical condition or ordinary acceptance as payment?”

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the extra cash made up of banknotes or coins that had been withdrawn from circulation and were no longer legal tender?"}
review:
The proposed question is not well supported and substantially repeats rejected territory. The history already says the extra cash was not invalid/non-spendable currency, and rejects it being legally excluded from ordinary payment for the proposed reasons. “Withdrawn from circulation and no longer legal tender” assumes precisely that kind of invalid status; the clues do not justify narrowing to it. Also, “no” to that earlier broad question does not establish what the cash was instead.

A safer discriminating question: “What specific legal consequence of the added cash changed what a potential attacker could infer?” Avoid proposing another specific currency mechanism until that distinction is clarified.

A better discriminator: “Did the notes’ special legal status come from how or why they were issued, rather than from being an obsolete Japanese issue?” This explores the remaining space without asserting a particular mechanism.

A safer discriminator is: “Could a potential attacker recognize the legally relevant status of the added notes from a visible feature printed on them?” That tests whether a notice or other marking mattered without presuming one.
